topic: Delegation: by, lazy, observable & custom delegates

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The `lazy` initializer runs only on the first read of `greeting`, which happens after `start` is printed. The result is cached, so the second read returns `Hello` without running the lambda again.

questions.question: In a Fragment you declare `private val vm: MainViewModel by viewModels()`. When is the ViewModel actually obtained from the `ViewModelProvider`?
options: When the Fragment is attached in `onAttach`
questions.explanation: `viewModels()` returns a `Lazy<VM>`, so nothing happens until `vm` is first read. That is also why touching `vm` before the Fragment is attached (e.g. in a field initializer that reads it) throws.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.code:
import kotlin.properties.Delegates

var age: Int by Delegates.vetoable(0) { _, old, new ->
    new >= old
}

fun main() {
    age = 10
    println(age)
    age = 5
    println(age)
    age = 20
    println(age)
}
questions.explanation: `vetoable` runs its callback before the change and only stores the new value if the lambda returns `true`. Assigning `5` when the old value is `10` returns `false`, so `age` stays `10`.

questions.question: The callback passed to `Delegates.observable` runs after the new value has already been stored, so it cannot reject the assignment.
questions.explanation: `observable` is notified after the change and its lambda returns `Unit`. If you need to reject a value, use `Delegates.vetoable`, whose lambda runs before the change and returns a `Boolean`.

questions.question: With Safe Args, a Fragment declares `val args: DetailFragmentArgs by navArgs()`. Where do the values come from?
options: The Fragment's `arguments` Bundle, read lazily on first access
The previous destination's `NavBackStackEntry`, copied over at navigation time
questions.explanation: `navArgs()` is a lazy delegate that calls `fromBundle(arguments)` the first time `args` is read. Navigation puts the destination's arguments into the Fragment's `arguments`, not the Activity intent; if `arguments` is null it throws.

options:
name: <none> -> Ann

Ann

name: Ann -> <none>
name: Ann -> Ann
Ann
questions.explanation: `observable` fires on every assignment, even when the new value equals the old one. It does not compare values, so add an `if (old != new)` check yourself if you only want real changes.

questions.question: Reading a `var count: Int by Delegates.notNull()` property before anything has been assigned to it returns `null`.
questions.explanation: The property type is the non-null `Int`, so it can never return `null`. Reading it before the first assignment throws `IllegalStateException` ("Property count should be initialized before get.").

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Delegating to a property reference (`by this::newName`) makes `oldName` an alias: every get and set goes straight to `newName`. It's a common way to rename a property while keeping the old name working, usually marked `@Deprecated`.

questions.question: A `CartFragment` and a `CheckoutFragment` live in the same Activity and must share one `CartViewModel` instance. Which declaration should both Fragments use?
questions.explanation: `activityViewModels()` scopes the ViewModel to the host Activity's `ViewModelStore`, so both Fragments get the same instance. `viewModels()` scopes it to each Fragment, giving two separate instances, and `lazy { CartViewModel() }` just creates a plain object that isn't kept across configuration changes.

questions.question: Which statements about `LazyThreadSafetyMode` are correct? Select all that apply.
options: With `PUBLICATION` the initializer may run more than once concurrently, but every caller sees the first value that was stored
`NONE` does no locking, so it is only safe when the property is accessed from a single thread
`NONE` throws an exception if two threads read the property
`PUBLICATION` guarantees the initializer runs exactly once
questions.explanation: `SYNCHRONIZED` (the default) locks so the initializer runs once. `PUBLICATION` lets racing threads each run it but publishes only the first result. `NONE` skips synchronization entirely; it doesn't detect multithreaded use, it just gives undefined behaviour, which is why it suits main-thread-only Android code.

questions.question: What happens when this code reads `c.retries`?
options: It fails to compile because the map has no `retries` key
questions.explanation: A map-backed property looks up `map[property.name]` on every read. If the key is missing it throws `NoSuchElementException` ("Key retries is missing in the map."). The compiler can't know the map's contents, so it compiles fine, and there is no default value.

questions.question: For `class Logged(private val inner: Repo) : Repo by inner`, where `Repo` is an interface, what does the compiler generate?
options: Forwarding methods for every `Repo` member it doesn't override, including ones with default bodies, calling `inner`
Forwarding methods only for abstract members, while members with default bodies use the interface's default implementation
A runtime proxy that uses reflection to dispatch calls to `inner`
A subclass of `inner`'s runtime class, so `Logged` inherits its implementation
questions.explanation: Delegation is resolved at compile time. Every member you don't override, even one with a default body, is forwarded to the delegate, so `inner`'s own overrides are used. No reflection or subclassing is involved, which is also why the delegate must be an interface.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `describe()` is forwarded to `inner`, and inside `Base` the call to `name()` goes to `Base.name()`, because `inner` knows nothing about `Logged`. Delegation isn't inheritance: your override only affects calls made through `Logged`, not calls the delegate makes on itself.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Both properties delegate to the same `Box` instance, and `Box` stores one value no matter which property is being accessed. Writing `b = 2` overwrites what `a` sees too. A delegate holding state needs one instance per property (or must key its storage by `p.name`).

questions.question: Why does this delegate store `userId` in the Fragment's `arguments` instead of a plain backing field?
options: `arguments` survives Fragment recreation, so `userId` outlives rotation and process death
Reading a Bundle is faster than reading a field
`ReadWriteProperty` can only write to a Bundle, because delegates can't have backing fields
It makes `userId` visible to the host Activity's `intent`, so the Activity can read it too
questions.explanation: After a configuration change or process death the system recreates the Fragment through its no-arg constructor and gives it back its saved `arguments`. A plain field would be reset. Using `property.name` as the key also means you don't have to keep key constants in sync.

questions.question: Given this SharedPreferences delegate, which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Every read of `darkMode` calls `prefs.getBoolean`; nothing is cached in the delegate
After `darkMode = true`, a read in the same process immediately returns `true`, even though `apply()` writes to disk asynchronously
The `key` parameter could be dropped by using `property.name` inside the delegate
`getValue` runs only once and its result is cached, like `lazy`
`darkMode` must be declared `lateinit` to use a delegate
questions.explanation: A delegate's `getValue`/`setValue` run on every access; only `lazy` adds caching. `apply()` updates the in-memory map right away and saves to disk in the background, so reads see the new value immediately. `lateinit` can't be combined with a delegate at all.

questions.question: Class delegation with `by` only works for interfaces: `class MyList(inner: ArrayList<Int>) : ArrayList<Int> by inner` does not compile.
questions.explanation: Kotlin only allows delegating the implementation of an interface. To wrap an `ArrayList` you'd write `class MyList(inner: MutableList<Int>) : MutableList<Int> by inner`, delegating the `MutableList` interface instead.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The `by inner` expression is evaluated once, during construction, and stored in a hidden field. Reassigning the `inner` property later doesn't change that field, so `greet()` still forwards to the original `En`.

questions.explanation: `provideDelegate` runs once per property while the object is being constructed, which is why both `bind` lines print before `created`, even for `subtitle`, which is never read. After that, each read calls only the returned delegate's `getValue`.
